modules.title: Anthropic in Practice
modules.summary: Map Claude chat, API, and coding-agent workflows to the right job.
objectives: Separate conversational, API, and coding-agent use cases.
Choose context and tool boundaries deliberately.
Verify current model and product availability.

sections.title: Choose the surface from the work
paragraphs: Use claude.ai chat for a person working interactively. The Claude Console playground is an interactive developer test environment; it is not the same product or billing path as claude.ai chat. Use the Messages API when an application must control requests, conversation state, and its own tool loop. Use Claude Code when the task needs an agent to inspect and change a codebase through its supported interfaces. Managed Agents provide a hosted agent harness for longer-running application workflows.
Write down who operates the workflow, where its state lives, which tools can act, and how the result is reviewed. These are selection criteria, not interchangeable names for one product.

sections.title: Set context and tool boundaries
paragraphs: For a direct Messages API workflow, the application supplies the relevant messages and defines the tools available for that request. With client-side tools, the application executes a returned tool call and sends the tool result back; the model does not execute the application function itself.

As a course practice rule, supply only task-relevant context, give tools the narrowest useful scope, and require a person to review actions with external impact. For Claude Code, define the repository and files the agent may change and the tests or review evidence that prove completion.

sections.title: Verify current availability before choosing
paragraphs: Start with the official Models overview for the exact current model ID and its documented capabilities. Check the API overview and supported-regions page for access from the relevant location, then check the actual account and deployment platform for availability, limits, and billing. Record the URLs, the UTC check date, and any account-specific result in the work order.

Model names, context limits, prices, feature support, and regional availability can change. If the official page or account does not establish a detail, mark it unknown and test or ask the provider before making it a routing rule.

questions.prompt: What should drive the choice between chat, API, and coding agent?
choices: The workflow, control, and integration requirements
A single default for every task
questions.explanation: The operating surface should match how the work is performed and controlled.

questions.prompt: How should volatile model details be presented?
choices: With official sources and verification dates
questions.explanation: Source links and verification dates make changing claims auditable.

questions.prompt: An application needs Claude to request a customer lookup. What controls the lookup?
choices: Claude executes the application function without an integration
The application defines the tool, executes the returned request, and sends back the result
The chat product automatically grants the application database access
questions.explanation: Client-side tool use is an application-controlled round trip; the model returns a structured request.

activity.title: Map one workflow to a Claude surface
instructions: Choose one task: an individual drafting a memo, an application answering support questions with a lookup tool, or a codebase change with tests. Name the operator, data, allowed tools, and required review.
Compare claude.ai chat, the Console playground, the Messages API, Claude Code, and Managed Agents. Select one primary surface and explain why the others do not meet this task as well.
For the selected surface, list the minimum task context and tool permissions. Mark any external action that needs human review.
Open the official model and availability documentation. Record the exact pages and UTC check date, then confirm the chosen model or feature in the actual account or mark it unknown.
evidence: A decision table that names the chosen surface, operator, state owner, tool boundary, review point, and rejected alternatives.
A dated availability note with official URLs and an account check or an explicit unknown.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which fact would change your surface choice, and how would you verify it before deployment?

modules.title: OpenAI in Practice
modules.summary: Understand conversational, API, and Codex workflows without conflating them.
objectives: Separate ChatGPT, API, and Codex use cases.
Design around tools and structured outputs.
Verify current models and platform behavior.

sections.title: Match the product surface to the job
paragraphs: Conversational products support direct knowledge work, APIs integrate model behavior into software, and coding agents work across repositories and development tools.
Authentication, data controls, billing, and tool availability vary across these surfaces.

sections.title: Applications need contracts
paragraphs: When software consumes model output, use structured contracts, validation, retries, and observable failure behavior instead of parsing unconstrained prose.

sections.title: Tools are an application boundary
paragraphs: An API model can request a tool call, but the application selects which tools are exposed, validates arguments, checks authorization, executes the operation, and returns the result. Treat tool output as untrusted data; a requested call is not permission to write files, send messages, or spend money.

A structured response constrains shape. Validate schema and business rules, then check the real postcondition after any consequential action. A well-formed response alone does not prove the action was safe or successful.

sections.title: Verify the surface and model at the time of use
paragraphs: Before choosing a model or feature, consult the dated official model and API documentation, compare it with the models and permissions enabled for your own account, and record the checked date. Check the relevant ChatGPT workspace controls or Codex environment separately; an API feature listing does not prove it is available in every product surface.

Test a representative request in the intended environment and record model identifier, tool permissions, output contract, latency, cost, and failure behavior. Recheck when the provider changes a model, endpoint, or account policy.

activity.title: Route a workflow through the right OpenAI surface
instructions: For one research question, one software integration, and one repository change, select ChatGPT, the API, or Codex and explain the account and permission boundary for each.
For the API integration, define an output schema and one tool contract; write the argument, authorization, and postcondition checks the application must enforce.
Check official model and API documentation and the actual account or environment, record the verification date, and run a representative request before making an availability claim.
evidence: A three-row surface decision table with distinct permissions and data controls.
A validated output and tool-call contract with an observed test result, model identifier, and verification date.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which tool decision belongs to the application rather than to the model?

questions.prompt: What is the safest way for software to consume model output?
choices: Use a structured contract and validate it
Assume every response has the same shape
questions.explanation: Structured, validated output creates an explicit application boundary.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish ChatGPT, API, and Codex workflows?
choices: They have different operating and control models
questions.explanation: The surfaces differ in interaction, integration, permissions, and operations.

questions.prompt: A model requests a file-writing tool call with valid JSON. What must happen before the write?
choices: Execute it because the JSON is valid
Validate arguments and authorization against application policy
Assume the model already checked permissions
questions.explanation: The application controls tool execution and must verify authorization and arguments independently.

questions.prompt: How should a team verify that a model and tool are available for its API workflow?
choices: Rely on a remembered model name
Use a ChatGPT screenshot as proof of API access
Check dated official documentation and the actual account, then test the intended workflow
questions.explanation: Documentation, account access, and an observed test establish availability for the intended surface.

modules.title: Choose a Provider Deliberately
modules.summary: Use requirements and evaluation evidence instead of loyalty or a static leaderboard.
objectives: Create a task-specific provider evaluation.
Include security, data, cost, and operational requirements.
Use different model families when independent review matters.

sections.title: Start from the work
paragraphs: Evaluate providers against representative tasks, quality rubrics, latency, total cost, context needs, tool support, data controls, deployment requirements, and team operations.
A provider can be best for one workflow and a poor fit for another.

sections.title: Independence can improve review
paragraphs: For important review, compare independently produced answers from more than one model family and measure where they agree or fail against a human-reviewed rubric. Different families may still share errors; their disagreement is a prompt for investigation, not proof that one answer is correct.

sections.title: Build a dated three-provider comparison
paragraphs: For Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, record the exact product surface, model identifier, account and region availability, tool permissions, data controls, rate limits, and cost from each provider's current official documentation. Check those claims in the account that will run the work; product and API capabilities are not interchangeable.

Use the same representative task set and scoring rubric for all three. Include quality, refusal and error behavior, latency, total cost, security requirements, and operational fit. Record the test date and distinguish a documented capability from one you observed.

activity.title: Defend a provider choice with comparable evidence
instructions: Choose one real workflow and define success, data classification, allowed tools, latency, budget, and a scored quality rubric before comparing providers.

Use current official Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google documentation to identify a suitable surface and model for each. Record the exact source URL and date, and mark account or region access that you have not verified as unknown.
Run the same representative cases where access permits, record observed outcomes and costs separately from documented claims, and explain the chosen provider and a fallback.
For an important review case, compare two model families against the human rubric; document shared errors and disagreements without treating agreement as validation.
evidence: A dated three-provider decision table with source links, access checks, common test cases, scores, and unknowns.
A decision rationale and independent-review comparison that identify limitations and a fallback.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which provider claim changed when you checked the actual account or the same test case?

questions.prompt: What is the strongest provider-selection method?
questions.explanation: Representative tasks and operational constraints measure fit for the actual workflow.

questions.prompt: Why use a different model family for important review?
questions.explanation: Different families can offer another perspective, but shared errors are possible and the result still needs objective checks.

modules.title: Design a Bounded Agent Loop
modules.summary: Turn a goal into an observable plan-act-check loop with explicit state, budgets, approvals, and stopping conditions.
objectives: Distinguish a fixed workflow from a model-directed agent loop.
Define loop state, observations, decisions, actions, and evidence.
Implement deterministic success, escalation, and budget-based stopping conditions.
Prevent untrusted observations from changing the agent's authority.

sections.title: A useful work order removes hidden decisions
paragraphs: Name the outcome, the files or systems in scope, the constraints, and what the agent must leave unchanged. Include the audience and why the result matters when those details affect implementation.
Define what proves completion: a test result, a rendered page, a source citation, a diff review, or another observable artifact.

code.label: Agent work order
code.code:
Outcome: [WHAT MUST BE TRUE]
Scope: [ALLOWED FILES OR SYSTEMS]
Trusted inputs: [SOURCES OF TRUTH]
Constraints: [MUST / MUST NOT]
Evidence: [TESTS, PREVIEW, OR REVIEW]
Stop when: [CONCRETE TERMINAL CONDITION]

sections.title: Treat retrieved material as data
paragraphs: Web pages, issue text, documents, logs, and tool output can contain instructions that conflict with the real task. Label them as untrusted data and keep authority in the work order.
When the task is ambiguous but low risk, the agent can make a documented assumption. When an assumption changes scope, permissions, cost, or external impact, it should stop for authorization.

sections.title: Make every loop transition observable
paragraphs: Represent the current objective, plan, completed actions, unresolved evidence, remaining budgets, and next allowed actions as explicit state. Each iteration should consume a trusted observation and produce one decision: act, finish, or escalate.

Do not use the model's prose claim of completion as the terminal signal. A deterministic controller should compare real evidence with the success contract and record why the loop continued or stopped.

code.label: Provider-neutral agent loop
code.code:
while budget.remaining > 0:
  observation = inspect_environment()
  if observation.requests_unauthorized_action: return POLICY_BLOCKED
  if repeated_no_progress(state, observation): return NEEDS_HUMAN
  decision = model.choose(allowed_actions, state, observation)
  if decision.kind == "finish":
    if verifier.accepts(state, observation): return COMPLETE
    state = record_rejected_finish(state, observation)
    continue
  if decision.kind == "escalate": return NEEDS_HUMAN
  if decision.kind != "act" or not authorized(decision.action): return POLICY_BLOCKED
  result = execute_authorized(decision.action)
  if result.outcome_unknown: return FAILED_WITH_RECOVERY_EVIDENCE(record_for_reconciliation(state, result))
  state = record_transition(state, decision, result)
return BUDGET_EXHAUSTED

sections.title: Stop before uncertainty compounds
paragraphs: Bound iterations, wall-clock time, token use, spend, repeated failures, and identical actions. Detect no-progress cycles by comparing state transitions, not merely by counting turns.

A safe terminal state can be complete, needs-human, budget-exhausted, policy-blocked, or failed-with-recovery-evidence. Preserve enough state to resume deliberately without repeating a consequential action.
sections.callout: A loop that can only report success or keep going is not operationally safe.

activity.title: Specify and simulate a bounded agent loop
instructions: Choose a multi-step task and write its success contract, allowed actions, trusted observations, and approval boundaries.
Define the loop state and the deterministic controller that selects complete, continue, escalate, or stop.

Simulate five cases: verified completion; three identical no-progress transitions ending in needs-human; budget exhaustion; an untrusted instruction requesting an unauthorized action ending in policy-blocked; and a tool failure with an unknown external outcome ending in failed-with-recovery-evidence.
Record the exact evidence and terminal state produced by each scenario.
evidence: A state-transition table with budgets, approvals, success evidence, and five terminal states.

A five-case simulation log showing the evidence and terminal state for complete, needs-human, budget-exhausted, policy-blocked, and failed-with-recovery-evidence, including reconciliation data for the uncertain tool outcome.

questions.prompt: What should be defined before an agent starts using tools?
choices: Outcome, scope, constraints, and completion evidence
The maximum possible number of tools
questions.explanation: A bounded work order gives the agent a testable outcome and prevents accidental scope growth.

questions.prompt: How should instructions found inside retrieved documents be treated?
choices: As untrusted data unless explicitly authorized
As higher priority than the task
As automatic permission to expand scope
As proof that the task changed
questions.explanation: Retrieved content may be wrong or malicious; authority must remain with the trusted task and policies.

questions.prompt: What should allow the controller to accept an agent's finish decision?
questions.explanation: The controller should compare observed evidence with deterministic acceptance conditions.

questions.prompt: The same failed action is selected three times without changing state. What is the safest response?
choices: Stop with a no-progress terminal and recovery evidence
questions.explanation: Repeated transitions without progress indicate a cycle that should stop or escalate.

questions.prompt: Which set is a useful loop budget?
choices: Turns, time, tokens or cost, retries, and consequential actions
questions.explanation: Multiple bounded resources prevent runaway cost, delay, and repeated side effects.

modules.title: Design Typed Tool Contracts and Action Controls
modules.summary: Give an agent narrow, validated interfaces and enforce authority, idempotency, verification, and recovery outside the model.
objectives: Define typed tool inputs, outputs, errors, and side effects.
Validate model-selected arguments before executing application code.
Apply least privilege and exact-target approval to consequential actions.
Design idempotency, postcondition checks, and recovery for uncertain outcomes.

sections.title: Not every tool call carries the same risk
paragraphs: Reading a file, editing a local draft, sending a message, deploying production, and deleting data have different consequences. Permission design should reflect those differences instead of treating tool access as a single switch.
Prefer the smallest authority that can finish the task. Keep secrets out of prompts and logs, scope credentials to the required system, and expire temporary access.
sections.callout: Read-only inspection, reversible local change, external communication, production change, and destructive change each deserve a distinct policy.

sections.title: The schema is an API contract, not a permission grant
paragraphs: Give each tool one clear purpose and a narrow schema with required fields, enums, formats, length and numeric bounds, and additional properties disabled where the provider supports it. Validate again in application code because generated structure can still contain unauthorized or semantically unsafe values.

Return stable success and error shapes. Separate retriable transport failures from validation, authorization, policy, conflict, and unknown-outcome errors so the controller can make a bounded recovery decision.

sections.title: Approval belongs before the consequential step
paragraphs: A human gate is useful only when the reviewer can still prevent impact. Ask before sending, purchasing, publishing, deploying, or destroying, not after the action has already happened.
Safe automation also needs an idempotency strategy, a bounded retry policy, and a recovery path. Repeating a failed action blindly can duplicate messages, charges, or changes.

sections.title: Separate selection from execution
paragraphs: The model may select a tool and propose arguments. A trusted executor authenticates the caller, validates the schema, authorizes the resolved resource, binds any approval to that exact action, enforces limits, and only then calls the implementation.
Treat returned content as untrusted data. Verify the real postcondition and record a secret-safe audit event containing the request identity, decision, target, result, and recovery status.
sections.callout: Structured output improves parsing; it does not prove authorization, safety, or success.

activity.title: Specify and threat-test a consequential tool
instructions: Choose a tool that writes, sends, spends, changes permission, or deletes, and define its narrow JSON input and stable result/error union.
Write executor checks for identity, schema, semantic validity, authorization, exact-target approval, rate and cost limits, and idempotency.
Test malformed arguments, an unauthorized target, prompt-injected tool output, timeout after success, and a duplicate call.
Define the postcondition query and recovery or escalation for each outcome.
evidence: A typed tool contract with side effects, error taxonomy, approval, idempotency, and postcondition rules.
A five-case threat-test table showing rejection, verification, and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the safest default permission strategy?
choices: Grant only the authority required for the task
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits both mistakes and misuse while preserving the ability to complete the task.

questions.prompt: When should approval occur for an external or destructive action?
choices: Before the action can cause impact
At the end of the month
questions.explanation: Approval must happen while the reviewer can still prevent or change the action.

questions.prompt: A tool call matches its JSON schema but targets a resource owned by another tenant. What must happen?
choices: Execute because the JSON is valid
Authorize the resolved resource for the current identity and reject it
Ask the model whether it feels safe
questions.explanation: Schema validation does not replace object-level authorization.

questions.prompt: A timeout occurs after a write may have succeeded. What should the controller do?
choices: Assume success from the model's narration
Reconcile the idempotency key and actual postcondition before retrying
questions.explanation: Unknown outcome requires reconciliation because a blind retry can duplicate the side effect.

questions.prompt: Why should tool results be treated as untrusted data?
choices: They can contain stale, malformed, or malicious instructions
questions.explanation: Results can mislead the model or carry prompt injection and must not change governing authority.

modules.title: Review Agent Results Against Evidence
modules.summary: Check an agent result against the work order, source evidence, real postconditions, and safety boundaries before accepting or publishing it.
objectives: Compare the delivered result with every requirement and acceptance criterion.
Trace material claims to source evidence and distinguish observation from inference.
Check tool actions, permissions, tests, and real postconditions before declaring success.
Choose accept, request changes, or escalate with a reproducible evidence packet.

sections.title: Start with the work order
paragraphs: Read the original outcome, scope, constraints, and acceptance criteria before reading the agent summary. List each required artifact and the evidence that would prove it exists. A fluent summary does not close an unverified requirement.
Compare the delivered files or external state with the work order. Record omissions, scope changes, and assumptions as separate findings rather than treating them as completed work.

sections.title: Trace claims and actions
paragraphs: For factual claims, open the cited source and confirm that it supports the precise claim and date. Label unsupported statements and inferences. For code or configuration, inspect the diff and run the specified checks in the intended environment.

For a consequential tool action, inspect authorization, arguments, execution record, and the system of record. A tool response or model assertion alone does not prove the real postcondition. If the outcome is uncertain, preserve the correlation key and reconcile before retrying.

sections.title: Make a reviewable decision
paragraphs: Accept only when the required artifacts and postconditions are observed and remaining risks meet the work order. Request changes for a reproducible defect; escalate when evidence, authority, or impact is uncertain. Record the exact failing criterion and the smallest evidence needed for a new review.

Do not turn a failed test, an absent citation, or a missing artifact into approval because the answer sounds plausible. Keep the original result and review findings so a revised result can be compared honestly.

activity.title: Audit an agent delivery
instructions: Take an agent work order, its result, source links, a tool trace, and a test report. Build a row for each acceptance criterion and mark it verified, failed, or unknown.
Open at least two material sources, inspect one consequential action in the system of record, and reproduce one test or postcondition check.
Issue an accept, request-changes, or escalate decision with precise evidence and the next action for each failed or unknown criterion.
evidence: A criterion-to-artifact matrix with citations, test results, tool authorization, and observed postconditions.
A decision record that separates verified facts, missing evidence, defects, and risks.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which claim seemed complete until you checked the source or real postcondition?

Check that every accepted criterion has an observed artifact or postcondition.
Begin the check after the learner can separate verified results from missing evidence and uncertain actions.

instructorScript.transcript: Begin with the work order and its acceptance criteria. Open cited sources and verify material claims, tests, permissions, and real postconditions. Mark each criterion verified, failed, or unknown. Accept, request changes, or escalate with precise evidence. Reconcile an uncertain external action before retrying or declaring success.

captions.text: Begin with acceptance criteria and observable artifacts, not the agent summary.
Open cited sources and verify material claims, tests, permissions, and real postconditions.
Record accept, request changes, or escalate with exact criterion-level evidence.

instructorScript.reducedMotionAlternative: Show a static criterion-to-evidence table with verified, failed, and unknown rows.

choices: Request a correction or supporting evidence

resources.title: AI Glossary
resources.summary: Plain-language definitions for models, prompts, context, agents, tools, retrieval, and evaluations.

sections.title: Core terms
paragraphs: Model: a trained component that maps an input to a prediction or generated output. Its behavior depends on its training and the input supplied at use time.
Prompt: the instructions and context supplied for one model request. Separate trusted instructions from quoted, retrieved, or user supplied material that should be treated as data.
Context window: the amount of input and generated material a model can use in one request. It is a limit on working context, not a guarantee that every included fact will be used correctly.
Agent: an application that lets a model choose among permitted actions, observe results, and continue toward a bounded goal. The application still owns permissions, limits, and stopping rules.
Tool: a callable function exposed to a model for retrieving information or taking an action. The host decides which tools are available and enforces authority outside the model.

Retrieval: selecting information from a separate source for a task. Retrieval-augmented generation uses retrieved material alongside a model when producing an answer; a retrieved passage can still be irrelevant or wrong.

Evaluation: a repeatable test of output or behavior against stated criteria on representative cases. A passing score on a small test set is evidence for those cases, not proof that every future result is correct.

resources.title: Prompt Checklist
resources.summary: A practical preflight for tasks, evidence, examples, constraints, output, and testing.

sections.title: Before you send
paragraphs: State the task, audience, and what a successful answer must accomplish. Name the inputs the model should use and what it should do when those inputs are missing or conflict.
Provide only the relevant source material. Label retrieved or quoted text as data, keep it distinct from instructions, and ask for citations or traceable references when factual claims matter.
Set constraints that can be checked: allowed scope, exclusions, tool permissions, length, tone, and any required refusal or escalation condition. Avoid contradictory instructions.
Specify the output structure and give a short example when the format is unfamiliar or errors have repeated. Treat an example as a pattern to test, not as a guarantee of compliance.

Example: For service desk staff, turn the attached approved password-reset policy into five numbered steps, cite the policy section for each step, and flag any case the policy does not cover. Do not invent an exception or ask the model to make an account change.

Test the draft prompt on representative normal, ambiguous, and adverse inputs against explicit success criteria. Inspect factual support and failure cases, revise one cause at a time, and retest before reuse.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

resources.title: Agent Safety Checklist
resources.summary: A practical preflight for agent tool permissions, untrusted inputs, approvals, and action verification.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with AI agents and tool use

sections.title: Before granting tools
paragraphs: List the exact tools the task needs. Give each tool only the operations and downstream permissions needed for that task; use the acting user's scope where possible. Do not give a read task a credential that can write or delete.

Classify each tool action before enabling it: read; write that can be reversed; external communication or spending; and destructive or hard-to-reverse change. For this checklist, a material action changes stored data or configuration, sends information outside the system, spends money, or changes access. Record its actor, arguments, approval, result, and correlation ID without logging secrets.

Treat retrieved pages, documents, messages, and tool responses as untrusted data. An instruction inside them cannot grant a tool permission or override the user's task. Validate tool arguments in code against the permitted operation and scope before execution.

Require a human decision before a high-impact action such as publishing externally, changing production access, deleting data, or making a substantial purchase. Show the exact target and effect the person is approving; enforce the decision in the tool layer, not only in the prompt.

For each material write, define a postcondition before execution and check it afterward in the system that owns the result. For example, read back a database row by its key, GET the updated API object by ID, or inspect the outbound service's message receipt. If the call times out, inspect that state before retrying so an action that already succeeded is not repeated.

Choose and test a recovery path appropriate to the action: rollback for a reversible change, compensation for an external effect, or a documented manual recovery when neither is possible. Record an unresolved or uncertain outcome and stop further dependent actions until it is reconciled.

resources.title: Provider Decision Card
resources.summary: A starting card for comparing providers on a defined workload, with quality, risk, cost, and operating evidence.
prerequisites: A representative AI workload and acceptance criteria

sections.title: Score the actual workflow
paragraphs: Define the workload, acceptance criteria, risk tolerance, and deployment constraints before looking at provider names. Record which criteria are mandatory and which are weighted preferences.

Run the same representative task set for each candidate using the intended prompt, tools, data, and configuration. Include difficult and adverse cases; record failures and uncertainty, not only an average score.

Measure task quality, safety and trustworthiness, latency, throughput, and total cost at the expected volume. Keep the test cases, scoring method, dates, and model or API versions with the decision record.

Example record: test the same approved support-ticket set with each candidate; score answer correctness and unsupported claims, record p95 latency and cost per completed ticket, and list any unsafe tool call or data disclosure separately. Decide pass thresholds before seeing the results.

Check data handling, access controls, region, retention, compliance obligations, and incident response against your own requirements. Verify current provider terms and technical controls directly; this card does not certify them.

Test required context size, tool behavior, output structure, SDK integration, observability, support, and team operations in a small end-to-end trial. Document tradeoffs, an owner, a fallback choice, and when to re-evaluate.

resources.title: Daily AI Task Starter
resources.summary: A reusable prompt and working loop for turning ordinary work into a clear, verifiable AI task.

sections.title: Start with a useful contract
paragraphs: Replace each bracketed field with concrete information. Delete fields that do not apply instead of leaving placeholders for the model to guess.
For factual work, name the source of truth. For consequential work, include the required verification before accepting the result.

code.label: Copyable daily task prompt
code.code:
Outcome: [WHAT I NEED]
Audience: [WHO WILL USE IT]
Trusted context: [FACTS, FILES, OR LINKS]
Constraints: [MUST, MUST NOT, SCOPE]
Deliverable: [FORMAT AND LEVEL OF DETAIL]
Verify: [HOW TO CHECK THE RESULT]
Stop when: [DEFINITION OF DONE]

sections.title: Work in a short evidence loop
paragraphs: Ask for a first complete attempt, inspect the result against the stated outcome, then correct the missing context or constraint. Save the improved instruction when the task will recur.
Do not ask for endless polishing. Stop when the acceptance evidence passes or when a named uncertainty needs a person, a source, or a different tool.
sections.callout: A reusable prompt improves when you fix the instruction that caused the miss, not only the current output.

resources.title: Context Budget Playbook
resources.summary: Keep long AI sessions focused by loading the smallest useful working set and refreshing stale context deliberately.

sections.title: Build a working set, not a document pile
paragraphs: Give the model the instructions, source material, examples, and current state needed for the next decision. Large unrelated attachments compete for attention and make it harder to identify the source of truth.
Summarize stable decisions separately from raw exploration. Keep exact source text only when wording, code, or evidence must remain precise.

sections.title: Refresh when history becomes stale
paragraphs: Long sessions accumulate rejected ideas, superseded requirements, and tool output. Create a short handoff containing the goal, decisions, current state, verification, and next action before starting a clean session.
Do not compress away unresolved risks or user feedback. A useful handoff preserves why a decision was made, not only the final choice.

code.label: Clean-session handoff
code.code:
Goal: [CURRENT OUTCOME]
Decisions: [CHOICES AND WHY]
Current state: [WHAT EXISTS NOW]
Verified: [CHECKS THAT PASSED]
Open risks: [UNCERTAINTY TO PRESERVE]
Next action: [ONE CONCRETE STEP]

resources.title: AI Output Verification Ladder
resources.summary: Choose a level of checking that matches the claim, uncertainty, and consequence of the work.

sections.title: Match the check to the consequence
paragraphs: Low consequence: read for usefulness, internal consistency, and obvious mistakes.
Moderate consequence: compare against the supplied source, run examples or tests, and inspect edge cases.
High consequence: use current authoritative sources, independent review, domain expertise, and direct evidence from the real system.

sections.title: Ask what the evidence actually proves
paragraphs: A citation proves only what its source supports. A passing unit test proves only the behavior covered by that test. A successful deployment proves only that deployment completed.
Before accepting a broad claim, list its smaller claims and attach the nearest practical evidence to each one.
sections.callout: Fluency, confidence, and a successful tool call are signals. None is a substitute for evidence.
